name: Tetracyclines
text:
Tetracyclines are a group of broad-spectrum antibiotics that are isolated from several species of Streptomyces bacteria or made semi-synthetically from them. They were discovered in the 1940s.

Tetracyclines have been used extensively to prevent and treat infections in humans and animals, and also at low doses in animal feed as growth promoters.

The group was given the number E701, but tetracyclines are antibiotics, not food additives.

name: Chlortetracycline
text:
Chlortetracycline is a tetracycline antibiotic and the first of the group to be identified. It was discovered in 1945 as a product of the soil bacterium Streptomyces aureofaciens.

In veterinary medicine it is used, for example, against conjunctivitis in cats, dogs and horses and against respiratory infections in calves, pigs and chickens. In humans it is used in a combination skin cream.

It has the number E702, but it is an antibiotic, not a food additive.

name: Oxytetracycline
text:
Oxytetracycline is a broad-spectrum tetracycline antibiotic, the second of the group to be discovered. It was first obtained from the soil bacterium Streptomyces rimosus and came into commercial use in 1950.

It is used in human medicine against infections such as those caused by Chlamydia and Mycoplasma, and in veterinary medicine. In the United States it is added to livestock feed to prevent disease in cattle and poultry.

It has the number E703, but it is a medicine, not a food additive.

name: Oleandomycin
text:
Oleandomycin is a macrolide antibiotic produced by strains of the bacterium Streptomyces antibioticus. It was discovered in 1954 and is weaker than the related antibiotic erythromycin.

It is used as a veterinary antibiotic in some countries, including for pigs and poultry.

It was given the number E704, but it is an antibiotic, not a food additive.

name: Penicillin G potassium
text:
Penicillin G potassium is the potassium salt of benzylpenicillin (penicillin G), a penicillin antibiotic used to treat bacterial infections such as pneumonia, strep throat and syphilis. Because it is poorly absorbed when taken by mouth, benzylpenicillin is generally given by injection into a vein or muscle.

It holds the number E705, but it is a medicine, not a food additive.

name: Penicillin G sodium
text:
Penicillin G sodium is the sodium salt of benzylpenicillin (penicillin G), a penicillin antibiotic that acts mainly against gram-positive bacteria. Benzylpenicillin is used to treat infections such as pneumonia, diphtheria, tetanus and syphilis, and is generally given by injection because it is poorly absorbed when taken by mouth.

It has the number E706, but it is an antibiotic, not a food additive.

name: Penicillin G procaine
text:
Penicillin G procaine is a salt of benzylpenicillin with the local anaesthetic procaine. It dissolves poorly, so after injection into a muscle it forms a deposit from which the antibiotic is released slowly over an extended period.

It is used against infections such as syphilis, anthrax, pneumonia and diphtheria, and was introduced for medical use in 1948.

It holds the number E707, but it is a medicine, not a food additive.

name: Penicillin G benzathine
text:
Penicillin G benzathine (benzathine benzylpenicillin) is a long-acting form of benzylpenicillin given by injection into a muscle; the benzathine component releases the penicillin slowly.

It is used to treat strep throat, diphtheria, syphilis and yaws, and to prevent rheumatic fever.

It has the number E708, but it is a medicine, not a food additive.

name: Spiramycin
text:
Spiramycin is a macrolide antibiotic that was isolated in 1954 as a product of the bacterium Streptomyces ambofaciens. It also acts against some parasites and is used in human medicine to treat toxoplasmosis and various soft-tissue infections.

Spiramycin was formerly authorised in the EU as an antibiotic additive in animal feed; that authorisation was withdrawn in 1998 to protect human health.

It has the number E710, but it is an antibiotic, not a food additive.

name: Virginiamycin
text:
Virginiamycin is a streptogramin antibiotic made up of two components, virginiamycin M1 and virginiamycin S1. It is used in livestock to prevent and treat infections and to speed up the animals' growth, and in the fuel ethanol industry to prevent microbial contamination.

In 1998 the EU withdrew its authorisation as a feed additive, because resistance to it could reduce the effectiveness of related antibiotics used in human medicine.

It has the number E711, but it is an antibiotic, not a food additive.

name: Flavomycin
text:
Flavomycin, also called bambermycin or flavophospholipol, is a complex of antibiotics, mainly moenomycins A and C, obtained from the bacteria Streptomyces bambergiensis and Streptomyces ghanaensis. It is intended solely for use in animal nutrition and has been fed to beef and dairy cattle, poultry and pigs to improve their performance.

Under EU feed law, antibiotics other than coccidiostats and histomonostats could no longer be used as feed additives from 1 January 2006.

It has the number E712, but it is not a food additive.

name: Tylosin
text:
Tylosin is a macrolide antibiotic produced by fermentation by the bacterium Streptomyces fradiae. It is used in veterinary medicine to treat bacterial infections in many species, for example respiratory infections and mastitis in cattle and pneumonia and enteritis in pigs. It has also been used as a growth promoter in animals raised for food. Given by mouth it can be fatal to horses.

In 1998 the EU withdrew the authorisation of tylosin phosphate as a feed additive to protect human health.

It has the number E713, but it is an antibiotic, not a food additive.

name: Monensin
text:
Monensin is a polyether antibiotic isolated from the bacterium Streptomyces cinnamonensis. It is an ionophore, a compound that carries metal ions such as sodium across cell membranes.

It is widely used in feed for beef and dairy cattle to prevent coccidiosis, a parasitic disease, and to prevent bloat, and as a coccidiostat for chickens and turkeys. It is also used in laboratory research. Monensin is especially toxic to horses, and accidental poisoning has killed horses.

It has the number E714, but it is not a food additive.

name: Avoparcin
text:
Avoparcin is a glycopeptide antibiotic, produced by the bacterium Streptomyces candidus, that acts against Gram-positive bacteria. It was added to livestock feed to promote growth in chickens, pigs and cattle, and to help prevent necrotic enteritis in poultry.

Because it is chemically similar to vancomycin, its use in animals raised concern about vancomycin-resistant bacteria. Denmark banned it as a feed additive in 1995 and Germany in 1996, and in 1997 the EU withdrew its authorisation as a precaution.

It has the number E715, but it is an antibiotic, not a food additive.

name: Salinomycin
text:
Salinomycin is an ionophore antibiotic that also acts as a coccidiostat. It is produced by the bacterium Streptomyces albus and is active against Gram-positive bacteria but not against fungi or Gram-negative bacteria.

It is used in chicken feed to control coccidiosis, a parasitic disease that damages the intestines of farm animals.

It has the number E716, but it is not a food additive.

name: Avilamycin
text:
Avilamycin is an antibiotic produced by the bacterium Streptomyces viridochromogenes; chemically it is an oligosaccharide derivative.

It has been used as an antibiotic additive in animal feed. Under EU feed law, antibiotics other than coccidiostats and histomonostats could no longer be used as feed additives from 1 January 2006.

It has the number E717, but it is an antibiotic, not a food additive.
